messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: Morning all. Quick round, then we can dig into the release.

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: Yesterday I finished the caching layer for the search endpoint. Response times dropped from 900ms to about 120ms on the staging box.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: That is a big win. Is it measured on the same query set as before?

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: Same fifty queries, same warm cache, ran it three times and took the median.

messages.speaker: Ines
messages.text: I spent yesterday chasing the signup bug. Turns out we were sending the confirmation email before the database transaction committed.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: So people clicked the link and the account did not exist yet.

messages.speaker: Ines
messages.text: Exactly. The email now goes out from an after-commit hook, so the row is always there by the time anyone clicks.

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: How many users hit that?

messages.speaker: Ines
messages.text: About 40 over two weeks. I have a script to resend to all of them once the fix is live.

messages.speaker: Raf
messages.text: I am still on the migration. Moving the events table to partitioned storage is slower than I hoped.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: What is the blocker?

messages.speaker: Raf
messages.text: The table is 400 million rows and copying it locks writes for too long. I am rewriting it to backfill in batches of fifty thousand.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: Do we need a maintenance window?

messages.speaker: Raf
messages.text: With the batched version, no. It runs in the background and we cut over with a rename at the end.

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: Have you tested the rollback path?

messages.speaker: Raf
messages.text: Not yet. That is today. I want to prove we can go back to the old table without losing writes.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: Good. Nothing ships without a tested way back.

messages.speaker: Ines
messages.text: On the release, are we still cutting on Thursday?

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: Thursday morning, so we have all day to watch it. Nothing goes out on a Friday.

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: The caching change needs a config flag flipped in production. I will document it in the release notes.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: Please make it default off, then we turn it on once we see the dashboards are calm.

messages.speaker: Ines
messages.text: What about the alerting? Last release we found out from a customer.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: That is on me. I am adding a page on error rate above two percent for five minutes straight.

messages.speaker: Raf
messages.text: Can we also alert on the queue depth? The backlog grew for an hour last time before anyone noticed.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: Yes, good call. Queue depth over ten thousand for ten minutes.

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: One more thing, the staging database ran out of disk again overnight.

messages.speaker: Raf
messages.text: That is the event table copies I keep leaving behind. I will add a cleanup step to the migration script.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: Fine. Anything anyone is stuck on that we have not covered?

messages.speaker: Ines
messages.text: Nothing from me.

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: All good.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: Then we are done. Raf, ping me when the rollback test passes.

messages.speaker: Raf
messages.text: Rollback test passed. I killed the backfill halfway, renamed back, and no writes were lost.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: How did you prove nothing was lost?

messages.speaker: Raf
messages.text: I ran a checksum of row counts and a sample of ids on both tables before and after. They matched exactly.

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: Did you test it under write load or on an idle database?

messages.speaker: Raf
messages.text: Under load. I had a script writing two hundred rows a second the whole time.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: That is the answer I wanted. Ship it.

messages.speaker: Ines
messages.text: While we are here, the signup fix is deployed and I resent to all 40 accounts. 31 have activated.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: What about the other nine?

messages.speaker: Ines
messages.text: Six bounced, so those addresses were wrong to begin with. Three have not opened it yet.

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: Do we chase them?

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: One reminder after seven days, then leave it. Chasing harder than that is spam.

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: The caching flag is on in production. Latency at the ninety fifth percentile went from 1.4 seconds to 180 milliseconds.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: Any errors?

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: Error rate is flat at 0.1 percent, same as before. Cache hit rate settled at 83 percent after an hour.

messages.speaker: Ines
messages.text: What happens on a cache miss under load? Do we stampede the database?

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: Good question. Right now yes, if a popular key expires we could get a hundred requests all rebuilding it at once.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: Then that is the next thing. A single flight lock so only one request rebuilds and the rest wait.

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: I will add it this week. It is about thirty lines.

messages.speaker: Raf
messages.text: Worth setting a jittered expiry too, so keys do not all expire on the same second.

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: Agreed, I will do both together.

messages.speaker: Ines
messages.text: We have a problem. The mobile app is showing stale prices for some users.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: How stale?

messages.speaker: Ines
messages.text: Up to six hours. One customer was quoted the old sale price and it did not match at checkout.

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: That smells like my cache. Prices are in the cached payload.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: Can you confirm before we assume?

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: Checking. Yes, confirmed. The price object is nested inside the product payload and I set a six hour expiry on the whole thing.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: So a price change does not invalidate the cache.

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: Right. Prices need to be either outside the cached payload or the cache needs invalidating on price write.

messages.speaker: Raf
messages.text: Invalidating on write is cleaner. Otherwise you have two sources of truth in the response.

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: Agreed. I will publish an invalidation event whenever a price row changes.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: How long to fix?

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: Today. And I will drop the expiry to fifteen minutes in the meantime so the blast radius shrinks now.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: Do the short expiry immediately, then the proper fix. What do we tell the customer who got the wrong price?

messages.speaker: Ines
messages.text: We honour the price they were shown. It was our error.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: Agreed. Every one of them, not just the ones who complain.

messages.speaker: Raf
messages.text: The partition migration is complete. All 400 million rows are across and the old table is dropped.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: How long did the backfill take in the end?

messages.speaker: Raf
messages.text: Nineteen hours, running at about six thousand rows a second. No downtime and no failed writes.

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: What did it do to query times?

messages.speaker: Raf
messages.text: Reporting queries that scanned a month of events went from 40 seconds to under two. Anything that scans a single day is roughly the same as before.

messages.speaker: Ines
messages.text: Is disk usage better or worse?

messages.speaker: Raf
messages.text: Slightly worse right now because each partition carries its own indexes, about eight percent more. It pays for itself once we start dropping old partitions.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: When do we start dropping them?

messages.speaker: Raf
messages.text: Retention is thirteen months. The first drop is in four weeks and it should free about sixty gigabytes.

messages.speaker: Ines
messages.text: Someone reported that search returns nothing for accented characters. Searching for a name with an acute accent gives zero results.

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: That is a normalisation problem. We are indexing the raw string and comparing against a folded query.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: So the index and the query disagree about what the same word looks like.

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: Yes. Both sides need the same unicode normalisation before they are compared.

messages.speaker: Raf
messages.text: Does that mean reindexing everything?

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: It does. About two hours for the full corpus, and search stays up because I can build into a new index and swap.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: Do it. How many users does this affect?

messages.speaker: Ines
messages.text: Hard to say precisely, but nine percent of our customer names contain a character outside plain ascii.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: That is far too many to leave broken.

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: The single flight lock is in. I load tested it with a thousand concurrent requests against one expired key.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: And?

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: One database query instead of a thousand. The other 999 waited an average of 40 milliseconds and got the shared result.

messages.speaker: Raf
messages.text: What happens if the one rebuilding request fails?

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: The lock releases and the next waiter takes over rebuilding, rather than all of them failing together.

messages.speaker: Ines
messages.text: Did you test that path or reason about it?

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: Tested. I made the rebuild throw deliberately and watched the second request pick it up.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: Good. That is the difference between a fix and a hope.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: Postmortem time on the stale price incident. What is the actual root cause?

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: The cache stored a composite object without thinking about which parts change at different rates.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: And the reason nobody caught it in review?

messages.speaker: Ines
messages.text: The review was on the caching mechanism, not on what was being cached. We looked at the how and not the what.

messages.speaker: Raf
messages.text: We also had no alert on price mismatch between the quote and the checkout. The customer was our monitoring.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: That is the part that bothers me most. Tom, can we compare quoted price to charged price and alert on divergence?

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: Yes, and it is cheap. Log both at checkout and alert if they differ by more than a penny.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: Do that. Three actions then: invalidation on write, which is done, the mismatch alert, and a review checklist item asking what changes at a different rate to the rest of this payload.

messages.speaker: Ines
messages.text: I will write the checklist item up.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: Nobody gets blamed for this one. The design was reasonable and the failure mode was not obvious. The gap was that we found out from a customer.

messages.speaker: Raf
messages.text: Heads up, the nightly reporting job has been failing silently for six days.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: Silently how?

messages.speaker: Raf
messages.text: It catches the exception, logs at debug level, and exits zero. So the scheduler thinks it succeeded.

messages.speaker: Tom
messages.text: That is worse than crashing.

messages.speaker: Raf
messages.text: Much worse. A crash would have paged someone on day one.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: What was the underlying error?

messages.speaker: Raf
messages.text: A column rename from the migration. The job still referenced the old name.

messages.speaker: Ines
messages.text: Why did the migration not catch that?

messages.speaker: Raf
messages.text: The job lives in a different repository and nothing links the two. There is no test that runs the reporting queries against the real schema.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: Then that is the fix, not just the column name. Add a schema contract test that runs in both repositories.

messages.speaker: Raf
messages.text: Agreed. And I am changing the catch to log at error and exit non zero, so it can never fail quietly again.

messages.speaker: Maya
messages.text: Six days of missing reports. Can we backfill?

messages.speaker: Raf
messages.text: Yes, the raw events are all there. I will rerun the six days tonight.
